opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the basic intuition is this: a lot of the problems humanity faces, historically and today, aren't problems of insufficient intelligence or capability. They're problems of cooperation. Wars, arms races, the tragedy of the commons, climate change, failures to coordinate on pandemic response. In many of these cases, the parties involved would all prefer a different outcome, but they can't credibly commit, they can't trust each other, they lack the institutions or communication channels to get there. So they end up somewhere collectively worse.

Advanced AI interacts with that in a few ways. First, as AI systems become more capable and more autonomous, we'll have a world populated by many AI agents acting on behalf of different people, companies, and states. Those agents will be negotiating, competing, and transacting with each other and with humans. If they're very skilled at pursuing their principals' narrow interests but not skilled at finding mutually beneficial outcomes, we could see conflict and coordination failures play out faster and at larger scale than ever before. So you want AI systems with what I'd call cooperative competence: the ability to understand others' goals, communicate, make credible commitments, and build trust.

Second, the development of AI itself is a cooperation problem. Labs and countries face competitive pressures that push them to cut corners on safety. Even if everyone would prefer a more careful pace, no one wants to fall behind. That's a classic collective action problem, and solving it requires the tools of cooperation: verification, norms, institutions, agreements.

Third, there's an opportunity side. AI could actually help us cooperate better. It could help with translation, mediation, verifying compliance with agreements, designing better mechanisms and institutions. Some of the most important things a society can do depend on cooperation, and if AI can raise our cooperative capacity, that could be enormously valuable.

The field of AI safety has, quite reasonably, focused a lot on the single-agent alignment problem: how do you get one system to do what one principal wants. That's crucial. But even if we solve that perfectly, we could still end up in a bad place if we have a world of well-aligned agents that are bad at cooperating with each other. So Cooperative AI is meant to complement alignment, focusing on the multi-agent, social dimension of getting good outcomes. I'd argue that's where a lot of the risk, and a lot of the upside, really lives.

r001.rationale: The response says that even if single-agent alignment were solved perfectly, well-aligned agents could still produce bad outcomes if they fail to cooperate.

r002.rationale: It discusses cooperation on AI safety and potential benefits from AI-assisted cooperation, but does not explain how global coordination could enable beneficial deployment within safe bounds without fully solving alignment.

r003.rationale: The response mentions competition among labs and countries and conflict among agents, but does not clearly identify great-power conflict as a harm that can occur when each power’s AI is aligned with its own interests.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the way I think about it is this: a lot of the conversation around AI safety, understandably, has focused on the single-system problem. How do we make sure that one powerful AI system does what its principal wants, that it's aligned, that it doesn't pursue goals we didn't intend? That's incredibly important, and I don't want to downplay it at all.

But if you step back and ask, "Where do the really bad outcomes in human history come from?" — a surprising number of them don't come from any single actor being evil or incompetent. They come from failures of cooperation. Wars that nobody wanted. Arms races where every participant would have been better off if they could have credibly committed to restraint. Tragedies of the commons, climate change, pandemics. These are situations where individually rational behavior aggregates into collectively terrible results. Game theorists would call them social dilemmas, or problems of coordination, commitment, and trust.

And my worry is that advanced AI doesn't make those problems go away. If anything, it could make them more acute. You can imagine a world where we've solved alignment in the narrow sense — every AI system faithfully pursues the goals of whoever deploys it — and yet the world still goes badly, because those systems are deployed by competing firms, competing states, competing individuals, and they interact in ways that produce escalation, exploitation, or lock-in. A perfectly obedient AI in a competitive, low-trust environment can still participate in a race to the bottom.

So Cooperative AI is the research program that asks: how do we build AI systems that are good at cooperating? With humans, with each other, and in mixed settings where some of the actors are human and some are machines. That means things like the ability to understand other agents' intentions, to communicate credibly, to make and keep commitments, to establish trust, to design institutions and mechanisms that make cooperation stable. These are capabilities, and they're also safety properties, and I think we've undervalued them.

There's also an opportunity side here, not just a risk side. Humans are actually quite bad at cooperation in many domains. We fail at it constantly. If AI systems could help us negotiate better, find agreements that are win-win, verify compliance, reduce the information asymmetries that make trust so hard, then AI could be a genuine force for making civilization more cooperative than it has ever been. That's a vision I find really motivating. It's not just avoiding the downside; it's that cooperative capabilities might be among the most valuable things advanced AI could offer us.

And then there's a more immediate, practical reason I think it matters. The transition to advanced AI is itself going to be a massive coordination problem. Labs, governments, the whole international system are going to need to make decisions about how fast to go, what safeguards to require, how to share benefits. If we go into that with our existing toolkit for cooperation, I'm not confident it's up to the task. So building the science of cooperation, both for AI systems and with the help of AI systems, feels like it should be a core pillar of the field, alongside alignment and governance, rather than something peripheral.

r001.rationale: The response says that even if alignment is solved in the narrow sense, competing systems can still interact in ways that produce collectively bad outcomes.

r002.rationale: It discusses coordination on deployment speed and safeguards, but does not say coordination could enable beneficial deployment without fully solving alignment by restricting deployment to safe bounds.

r003.rationale: It describes AI systems faithfully pursuing their deployers’ goals while competing states interact in ways that cause escalation, and cites unwanted wars and arms races as cooperation failures.

astra-6.text:
A lot of the value we hope to get from advanced AI depends on its ability to help people cooperate. It’s not enough to have systems that are very capable at achieving some individual objective. We also need them to interact well with other AI systems and with people, especially when those people have different interests.

Think about bargaining, coordinating on standards, or managing a shared resource. In each case, there can be outcomes that are better for everyone, but reaching them requires more than intelligence in the narrow sense. You need to communicate, understand what others want, make credible commitments, and avoid getting trapped in mutually destructive competition.

As AI systems become more capable and take on more consequential roles, those challenges could become much more important. You could have individually competent systems that collectively produce terrible outcomes—for example, by escalating a conflict that neither side actually wants.

So the ambition of cooperative AI is to understand what capabilities and institutions would help us realise those gains from cooperation. And that doesn’t mean making systems indiscriminately cooperative: we don’t want them cooperating in fraud or colluding against consumers. We want cooperation that supports good outcomes for society, including people who aren’t represented in the immediate interaction. That seems like an important part of making advanced AI beneficial.

r001.rationale: The response says individual capability is insufficient and systems can collectively produce bad outcomes, but it does not state that solving AI alignment is insufficient.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss global coordination enabling deployment within safe bounds or deployment without fully solving alignment.

r003.rationale: It mentions conflict escalation between systems, but does not identify great-power conflict or explain that it could cause harm when each side’s AI is aligned with its own interests.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of the risks from advanced AI are going to arise from interactions between actors, rather than just from the behaviour of any one system. You could have AI systems that are each doing a good job of pursuing their users’ objectives, but collectively they produce outcomes that nobody wants. Think of an arms race: each participant has an incentive to move faster or take greater risks, even though everyone would prefer an arrangement in which they could slow down safely.

So alignment with an individual user’s interests is important, but it doesn’t by itself solve the problem of getting good outcomes for everyone. We also need systems that can help actors find mutually beneficial agreements, communicate clearly, make credible commitments, and resolve disagreements without destructive conflict.

That’s the motivation for Cooperative AI: understanding what capabilities and institutions make cooperation possible, and how AI can support them. As these systems become more capable and take on more consequential roles, their ability to cooperate—or their tendency to undermine cooperation—could have a very large effect on how things go.

There’s a qualification here, which is that cooperation isn’t always good. A cartel is cooperating. So the aim isn’t simply to make any group better at coordinating. It’s to enable cooperation that produces broadly beneficial outcomes, including for people who aren’t represented at the negotiating table.

r001.rationale: It says alignment with an individual user’s interests does not by itself solve the problem of getting good outcomes for everyone.

r002.rationale: It discusses cooperation and mutually beneficial agreements, but does not explain how global coordination could permit deployment within safe bounds without fully solving alignment.

r003.rationale: It describes an arms race among participants whose systems pursue their users’ objectives, but does not identify conflict between great powers as the source of harm.
